report.answer_text:
Solar Orbiter captured the first clear images of the Sun’s south pole in March 2025. Its magnetic maps revealed patches of both north and south magnetic polarity side by side, rather than one dominant polarity. ESA released the images on June 11, 2025. (esa.int)
That patchwork is characteristic of solar maximum, the active phase of the Sun’s roughly 11-year cycle when its global magnetic field reverses. (esa.int)

quotes.text: Thanks to its newly tilted orbit around the Sun, the European Space Agency-led Solar Orbiter spacecraft is the first to image the Sun’s poles from outside the ecliptic plane.

The video above compares Solar Orbiter’s view (in yellow) with the one from Earth (grey), on 23 March 2025. At the time, Solar Orbiter was viewing the Sun from an angle of 17° below the solar equator, enough to directly see the Sun’s south pole.
The collage above shows the Sun’s south pole as recorded on 16–17 March 2025, when Solar Orbiter was viewing the Sun from an angle of 15° below the solar equator.

pages.quote_reason: The quotes back that Solar Orbiter imaged the Sun's south pole in March 2025 from below the solar equator, but they never state that these were the first clear images of the south pole specifically, though they do say it was the first to image the poles from outside the ecliptic plane.
pages.page_reason: The page states that Solar Orbiter is the first to image the Sun's poles from outside the ecliptic, shows south pole images recorded 16–17 March 2025 and a view on 23 March 2025, and calls them humankind's first-ever views of the pole, though it does not explicitly say they are 'clear' images.

These groundbreaking new observations are also key to understanding the Sun’s magnetic field and why it flips roughly every 11 years, coinciding with a peak in solar activity.
